newsitem.title: UK: Railtrack says results show progress.
newsitem.headline: Railtrack says results show progress.

text.p: British railways owner Railtrack Plc on Friday announced a 12 percent rise in operating profits in its first results since privatisation, and vowed to defy its critics and create the best railway in the world.
Operating profits rose to 169 million pounds ($282 million) from 151 million a year earlier and the company declared its first dividend of 7.3 pence a share.
The partly-paid share price jumped 37p on the results in a generally firmer market to 322p. This compares to an offer price in May of 190p for the general public and 200p for institutions.
"This has been a landmark half-year for Railtrack. The success of our flotation in May has been accompanied by real progress in the renaissance of the railways," chairman Robert Horton said.
"We will continue to give high priority to maintaining our close relationship with the rail regulator to deliver the world's most safe, reliable and efficient commercial railway."
The prospectus for Railtrack's selloff had said it would have paid an interim dividend of 6.85 pence a year ago and analysts expected to see between 7.3 and 7.45 pence this time.
The dividend was covered by earnings up four percent at 29 pence a share against a proforma 27.8 pence a year ago.
Railtrack finance director Norman Broadhurst said that the company had promised "a progressive dividend policy" and earnings cover would be addressed "once we have a track record."
The company asked to be left alone by opponents of the share sell-off to let it now prove that Britain's railways can be run more effectively in the private sector.
"I want people to judge us by what we achieve in practice," chief executive John Edmonds told a news conference.
Britain's opposition Labour Party has said if it wins the next general election it will make Railtrack spend more on new track and signalling.
It has also threatened to levy a windfall tax on an as yet unspecified number of former state-owned utilities which it says were sold off too cheaply by the Conservative government.

"Railtrack's position is that we want to deliver to our customers in a satisfactory way and then, we feel, the regulator and the politicians will understand our role and not seek to interfere with a successful company," Edmonds said.

He added: "If the Labour Party has the objectives they state, which are higher levels of investmeent and a better quality of service, I hope they will look at what we are actively achieving and conclude that Railtrack is the sort of company they can live comfortably with."
